claimSpecificEvidence.claim: The FDA-approved Victoza (liraglutide) label states it is indicated (1) as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients aged 10 years and older with type 2 diabetes mellitus, and (2) to reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus and established cardiovascular disease.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: High-confidence regulatory, label or agency fact backed by an authoritative source.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: The FDA-approved Saxenda (liraglutide 3 mg/day) label states it is indicated, in combination with a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity, to reduce excess body weight in (a) adults and pediatric patients aged 12 years and older with body weight above 60 kg and obesity, and (b) adults with overweight plus at least one weight-related comorbid condition.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: High-confidence regulatory, label or agency fact backed by an authoritative source.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Both Victoza and Saxenda (liraglutide) carry an FDA boxed warning that liraglutide causes thyroid C-cell tumors in rodents at clinically relevant exposures, with human relevance undetermined; liraglutide is contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) or Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2), and in patients with serious hypersensitivity to liraglutide or its excipients.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: High-confidence regulatory, label or agency fact backed by an authoritative source.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: The Victoza label documents reports of acute pancreatitis (including fatal and non-fatal hemorrhagic or necrotizing pancreatitis), gastrointestinal adverse reactions (sometimes severe), acute gallbladder disease (cholelithiasis/cholecystitis), increased hypoglycemia risk when combined with insulin or an insulin secretagogue, and rare reports of pulmonary aspiration during elective surgery in patients receiving GLP-1 receptor agonists.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: High-confidence regulatory, label or agency fact backed by an authoritative source.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In the LEADER trial (liraglutide vs. placebo added to standard care in 9,340 adults with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk), the primary composite cardiovascular outcome (death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke) occurred in fewer patients in the liraglutide group (608 of 4,668 patients, 13.0%) than in the placebo group (694 of 4,672 patients, 14.9%), hazard ratio 0.87 (95% CI 0.78-0.97, p=0.01 for superiority); this trial underlies Victoza's cardiovascular risk-reduction indication.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Consistent human or authoritative evidence for the stated claim (was Strong).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: A CADTH clinical review of Saxenda's pivotal SCALE phase 3 trials found statistically significant placebo-adjusted body-weight reductions with liraglutide 3 mg, including a treatment difference of −5.39% (95% CI −5.82 to −4.95, p<0.0001) in the main trial (Study 1839), with odds of achieving ≥5% weight loss about 4.8-fold higher than placebo (OR 4.80, 95% CI 4.12–5.60, p<0.0001). The same review flagged evidence gaps: underrepresentation of patients with BMI 27 to <30 kg/m2, a lack of comparative (head-to-head) evidence, and trial populations that were predominantly White and female, limiting generalizability.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Consistent human or authoritative evidence for the stated claim (was Strong).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: FDA has warned companies that illegally sold unapproved GLP-1-class drugs falsely labeled 'for research purposes' or 'not for human consumption' directly to consumers with dosing instructions, and states these products are of unknown quality. FDA also states that compounded drug products are not FDA-approved and have not undergone FDA review for safety, effectiveness, or quality. No human outcome data support unsupervised, non-prescription self-administration of liraglutide-class products obtained through these channels, and such use falls outside any FDA-approved label.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim describes promotional or online certainty beyond the cited evidence.

evidenceGaps: Real-world compounded or research-labeled liraglutide-class injectables lack FDA review for quality; supply-chain authenticity is a persistent problem.

controversies: Illegal online sellers market GLP-1 injectables without valid prescriptions, sometimes as research peptides.

Illegal online sellers market GLP-1 agonist injectables — the drug class that includes liraglutide — without requiring a valid prescription, and some sellers evade enforcement by labeling products 'peptides' intended 'for research purposes only' and 'not for human consumption.' Substandard and falsified GLP-1 products have been identified in multiple countries. Separately, FDA states that compounded drug products are not FDA-approved and have not undergone FDA review for safety, effectiveness, or quality. No human outcome data support unsupervised, non-prescription self-administration of liraglutide-class products obtained through these channels, and such use falls outside any FDA-approved label.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Controlled human trial evidence specific to sermorelin/GHRH(1-29) in adults is limited: a small 1997 trial (11 healthy men, 64-76 years, 6 weeks of single nightly GHRH(1-29) injections) found improvement in only 2 of 6 strength measures and one muscle-endurance measure, with no change in DEXA-measured lean mass or fat, weight, BMI, or waist-to-hip ratio; a separate 2006 trial (89 healthy older adults, 6 months of daily GHRH treatment) found improved cognition on some measures (novel problem-solving, psychomotor/processing speed, working memory) but no improvement on 3 of 6 cognitive tests and no effect on sleep. claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Sermorelin is promoted online for anti-aging, restoring natural growth-hormone production, well-being, lean body mass, insulin sensitivity and libido. The libido, insulin-sensitivity, general-well-being, and 'restores natural hGH production'/anti-aging framing are not supported by any controlled human trial identified for sermorelin/GHRH(1-29). The lean-body-mass claim specifically is also not supported: the one located controlled trial that measured body composition (Vittone et al. 1997, 11 elderly men) found no change in DEXA-measured lean mass or fat, though it did find improvement on 2 of 6 strength measures and one muscle-endurance measure. A separate controlled trial (Vitiello et al. 2006, 89 older adults) found improved cognition on some measures, which is not among the marketing claims evaluated here. None of this rises to evidence for the marketing claims as stated, and sermorelin's sole historical FDA-approved indication was pediatric growth hormone deficiency, now discontinued; these marketing claims should not be read as proven benefits.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) briefing document evaluating MOTS-c (free base) and MOTS-c acetate for the 503A Bulks List, FDA staff state they did not identify any clinical studies or human exposure data for MOTS-c via any route of administration, and that both forms are not well-characterized from a physical/chemical characterization standpoint due to unavailable data on impurities, aggregates, and endotoxins; FDA staff recommended against adding either form to the list. The Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee discussed MOTS-c on July 23, 2026; FDA had not published official minutes or a vote record at this review, so the outcome is unknown here (reported only by non-regulator sources). An advisory committee vote is not a listing decision: FDA must still complete rulemaking before MOTS-c could be compounded under 503A.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: No published controlled human study of exogenously administered MOTS-c establishing efficacy for metabolic, fat-loss, exercise-performance, or anti-aging outcomes was identified; the only human MOTS-c data located is observational measurement of endogenous (naturally produced) circulating MOTS-c rising during exercise, and FDA's own review found no clinical studies or human exposure data for administered MOTS-c. The physical-capacity and healthspan benefits reported for MOTS-c are from mouse studies only.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Only mechanistic or preclinical rationale found (was Insufficient).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: An investigational Phase 2a randomized, placebo-controlled trial (NCT07505745) is recruiting adults aged 18-65 with BMI 27-40 kg/m2 and documented prediabetes to receive investigational MOTS-c or matching placebo via subcutaneous injection once daily for 12 weeks alongside standardized lifestyle counseling, to evaluate improvement in insulin sensitivity; results are not yet available.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: No adequate source-verified support found for the specific claim (was Insufficient).

FDA's briefing found no clinical studies or human exposure data for administered MOTS-c, and WADA lists MOTS-c as a prohibited AMPK activator (S4.4.1). evidenceGaps: No published controlled human study of exogenously administered MOTS-c establishing efficacy for metabolic, fat-loss, exercise-performance, or anti-aging outcomes was identified; the only human MOTS-c data located is observational measurement of endogenous (naturally produced) circulating MOTS-c rising during exercise, and FDA's own review found no clinical studies or human exposure data for administered MOTS-c. The physical-capacity and healthspan benefits reported for MOTS-c are from mouse studies only.
Community-reported doses: n/a (no citable source).
controversies: Gray-market peptide vendor content promotes self-administered MOTS-c dosing protocols (e.g., titrating from roughly 2.5-5 mg subcutaneously several times weekly up to a 10 mg five-times-weekly maintenance regimen, timed 30-60 minutes before exercise) and attributes fat-loss, exercise-mimetic, and anti-aging benefits to it, while citing mouse data and a single small uncontrolled/early-phase human observation as support; this marketing framing outruns the human evidence base, which FDA and the primary literature reviewed here describe as absent for administered MOTS-c.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: FDA states it has approved no drug products containing thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin) and that it is not approved in the United States, Japan, or Europe (except Italy). A 2009 review reports approval in over 35 countries for hepatitis B and C and as an immune adjuvant; FDA says it could not independently verify those approval claims.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: High-confidence regulatory, label or agency fact backed by an authoritative source.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: FDA's evaluation of thymosin alpha-1 (Tα1, free base and acetate) for the 503A compounding Bulks List found that a balancing of the four evaluation criteria weighs against adding it, citing insufficient physicochemical characterization, an immunogenicity risk potentially amplified by aggregation and peptide-related impurities, and a proposed injectable concentration (3 mg/mL) that exceeds Ta1 free base's aqueous solubility (2 mg/mL); the nomination was subsequently withdrawn and FDA is evaluating the substance at its own discretion rather than under a completed rulemaking.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: High-confidence regulatory, label or agency fact backed by an authoritative source.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: FDA's bulk drug substance evaluation flags a potential safety concern specific to immunosuppressed patients: thymosin alpha-1's immune-stimulating activity could cause or worsen acute or chronic graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) and lead to engraftment failure in hematopoietic stem cell transplant (HSCT) recipients.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Human evidence exists but is not settled (was Moderate).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin) is a synthetically manufactured 28-amino-acid acetylated polypeptide identical to a naturally occurring human thymic peptide; it is described as activating toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) signaling on dendritic cells, driving Th1 polarization and T-cell maturation as part of coordinated adaptive immune responses.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Human evidence exists but is not settled (was Moderate).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In the largest and most rigorous published human efficacy trial - TESTS, a multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in 1,106 adults with sepsis across 22 Chinese centers - subcutaneous thymosin alpha-1 every 12 hours for up to 7 days did not reduce 28-day all-cause mortality versus placebo (23.4% vs 24.1%; hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.77-1.27, p=0.93), and secondary/safety outcomes showed no significant differences between groups.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim reports a negative or conflicting human finding.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: An earlier, smaller multicenter randomized controlled trial (ETASS, six Chinese hospitals, n=361 ICU patients with severe sepsis, 2008-2010) reported a numerically lower 28-day death rate with thymosin alpha-1 added to conventional therapy versus conventional therapy alone (26.0% vs 35.0%; relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.54-1.02), a difference that did not reach conventional statistical significance, alongside greater improvement in monocyte HLA-DR expression (an immune-function marker) in the treatment group.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim reports a negative or conflicting human finding.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Thymosin alpha-1 is marketed online for immune 'optimization', autoimmune disease, inflammation, cancer support and longevity uses; FDA notes a website advertising a compounded product as 'FDA-approved' although FDA has approved none. The largest placebo-controlled human trial in a systemic-immune indication (TESTS, sepsis) found no mortality benefit, and no controlled human evidence for general immune optimization, anti-aging or wellness use in healthy adults was identified.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim describes promotional or online certainty beyond the cited evidence.

evidenceGaps: Thymosin alpha-1 is marketed and discussed online as having been "long recognized for modifying, enhancing, and restoring immune function," with popular interest extending to autoimmune disease management, general inflammation reduction, cancer support, and longevity-adjacent uses such as long COVID; the only large, rigorous, placebo-controlled human trial identified for a systemic-immunomodulation indication (sepsis) found no mortality benefit, and consumer-facing sources themselves acknowledge that findings for these broader immune/longevity uses are based on small trials and that "more research is needed." No controlled human evidence for general immune optimization, anti-aging, or wellness use in healthy adults was identified in this review.
controversies: Discordance between earlier smaller sepsis signals (ETASS) and the larger negative TESTS trial complicates efficacy interpretation.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: AC-262536 (Accadine/Accadrine, CAS 870888-46-3, C18H18N2O, MW 278.4) is a non-steroidal selective androgen receptor modulator originally developed by Acadia Pharmaceuticals; it exhibits endo-exo isomerism with the endo form being pharmacologically active, and it is not an approved pharmaceutical product.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: High-confidence regulatory or label fact backed by an authoritative source.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In a cell-based functional assay, AC-262536 was identified as a potent, selective androgen-receptor ligand acting as a partial agonist relative to testosterone (reported Ki approximately 5 nM); in castrated male rats it produced anabolic effects on the levator ani muscle (reported at roughly 66% of testosterone's maximal effect) while producing substantially weaker effects on prostate gland weight (roughly 27% of testosterone's maximal effect), indicating tissue-selective activity in animal models. This is preclinical (in vitro and rodent) evidence only and has not been demonstrated in humans.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Preliminary human evidence with documented limits (was Limited).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: AC-262536 has no approved medical use and is not a licensed pharmaceutical product in the United States; FDA states that SARMs as a class 'are not FDA approved' and 'cannot be legally marketed in the U.S. as a dietary supplement or drug at this time,' and AC-262536 has additionally been documented as encountered in the illicit/novel-designer-drug market.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: High-confidence regulatory, label or agency fact backed by an authoritative source.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: FDA has warned that SARMs as a class are 'associated with serious or life-threatening health problems,' specifically citing increased risk of heart attack or stroke and liver injury/acute liver failure, along with psychosis/hallucinations, sleep disturbances, sexual dysfunction, infertility, pregnancy/miscarriage risk, and testicular shrinkage; this warning targets the SARM drug class broadly (including products marketed to teens and young adults) and is not derived from AC-262536-specific human safety data, which does not exist.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim reports a negative or conflicting human finding.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: No published human clinical trials of AC-262536 exist; all pharmacological and efficacy data available come from a single in vitro/rodent characterization study. Human safety, dosing, and efficacy are entirely unestablished.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Only mechanistic or preclinical rationale found (was Insufficient).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: AC-262536/Accadrine is marketed online (as a bodybuilding/'SARM' supplement) with claims that it builds muscle and strength, raises testosterone, 'slows down the onset of Alzheimer's disease,' shrinks the prostate favorably, and produces 'no exogenous side effects' — claims drawn entirely from a single rodent/in-vitro pharmacology study and not supported by any human data; the marketing does not disclose the absence of human trials or FDA's class-wide SARM safety warnings.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim describes promotional or online certainty beyond the cited evidence.

evidenceGaps: No published human clinical trials of AC-262536 were identified; pharmacology rests on limited preclinical work (including PMID 18164613 characterization).

No published human clinical trials of AC-262536 exist; all pharmacological and efficacy data available come from a single in vitro/rodent characterization study. Human safety, dosing, and efficacy are entirely unestablished.
controversies: Online marketing claims muscle, testosterone, and neurologic benefits from rodent data and omit FDA class-wide SARM warnings and the absence of human trials.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In ELAINE 1, an open-label, randomized, phase II, multicenter trial in 103 patients with ER+/HER2- metastatic breast cancer harboring an ESR1 mutation who had progressed on prior aromatase-inhibitor-based therapy, oral lasofoxifene 5 mg daily (n=52) numerically improved median progression-free survival versus intramuscular fulvestrant 500 mg (n=51) - 24.2 weeks (~5.6 months) vs 16.2 weeks (~3.7 months) - with a hazard ratio of 0.699 (95% CI 0.434-1.125); the difference did not reach statistical significance (p=0.138). Both arms showed grade 3/4 toxicity in roughly 20% of patients with no unexpected safety signals; the most frequent lasofoxifene adverse events were nausea, fatigue, arthralgia, and hot flushes.

mechanism.mechanismSummary: LGD-3303 is a nonsteroidal, orally bioavailable SARM that binds the androgen receptor with high in vitro affinity (Ki = 0.9 nM) and potently activates AR-mediated transcription (EC50 = 3.6 nM, 134% efficacy relative to dihydrotestosterone), while showing much weaker affinity for the mineralocorticoid, glucocorticoid, and progesterone receptors (Ki = 1261, 581, and 136 nM respectively).
primaryMechanisms: LGD-3303 is a nonsteroidal, orally bioavailable SARM that binds the androgen receptor with high in vitro affinity (Ki = 0.9 nM) and potently activates AR-mediated transcription (EC50 = 3.6 nM, 134% efficacy relative to dihydrotestosterone), while showing much weaker affinity for the mineralocorticoid, glucocorticoid, and progesterone receptors (Ki = 1261, 581, and 136 nM respectively).

In castrated male rats (an androgen-deficiency model), oral LGD-3303 at 1 mg/kg/day completely prevented loss of levator ani muscle weight and acted as a partial agonist on prostate and preputial gland tissue; local tissue drug concentrations were reportedly higher in prostate than in the more strongly responding levator ani muscle, indicating the tissue selectivity is not explained by differential drug distribution. This is preclinical rodent evidence only and has not been demonstrated in a human clinical study.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In a castrated-rat model of androgen deficiency, LGD-3303 had potent activity on levator ani muscle but acted as a partial agonist on prostate and preputial gland, and never stimulated ventral prostate above intact levels; local drug concentrations were higher in prostate than in muscle, so the tissue selectivity is not explained by drug distribution. This is rodent evidence only; no human study exists.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: LGD-3303 was developed by Ligand Pharmaceuticals and published only in preclinical (rat) studies of muscle, prostate and bone. No human clinical trial or marketing approval was found in any registry or regulator source reviewed; FDA states SARMs cannot be legally marketed as supplements or drugs.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Human evidence exists but is not settled (was Moderate).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: FDA classifies SARMs as a drug class - which includes LGD-3303 by chemical and pharmacological category - as unapproved products that "cannot be legally marketed in the U.S. as a dietary supplement or drug at this time," and warns that SARM use is associated with increased risk of heart attack or stroke and liver injury/acute liver failure, among other serious effects. No FDA warning letter or enforcement action naming LGD-3303 specifically was located in this session's search of fda.gov.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: High-confidence regulatory, label or agency fact backed by an authoritative source.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: NIH's LiverTox reference describes a distinctive bland cholestatic drug-induced liver injury pattern documented with SARM use as a class: onset roughly 2-3 months after starting, presenting with fatigue, anorexia, dark urine, and jaundice, with moderate bilirubin elevation (reported 4-8 mg/dL initially) but only 2-5x-normal aminotransferase elevation, and a prolonged but usually self-limited course of about 1-6 months, occasionally with bilirubin cast nephropathy requiring temporary dialysis in severe cases. The compounds specifically named in LiverTox's case-report basis are ligandrol (LGD-4033), enobosarm/ostarine, vosilasarm/RAD-140, andarine, and YK-11; LGD-3303 is not individually named among the documented case reports in this reference, despite sharing the same androgen-receptor mechanism class.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Support is user, community or case reports, not generalizable evidence.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: The WADA 2026 Prohibited List (S1.2 Other anabolic agents) prohibits selective androgen receptor modulators 'including, but not limited to' the examples it names, so LGD-3303 falls within the prohibited SARM class even though it is not named individually. Anti-doping researchers have profiled LGD-3303 metabolites in horses and propose a monohydroxylated metabolite as a doping-control target.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Mechanistic or preclinical support without direct human outcome evidence (was Moderate).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: LGD-3303 is sold online as a 'research use only' chemical while sellers highlight rat muscle data in ways that imply bodybuilding benefit. No human efficacy or safety trial, case series or regulator clinical data for LGD-3303 was located; FDA warns against SARM use, and LiverTox documents liver injury with the SARM class. Muscle-building, bone or performance claims are not supported by human evidence. Community-reported doses: n/a (no citable source).
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Support is user, community or case reports, not generalizable evidence.

evidenceGaps: No human clinical trial, case series, or compound-specific FDA enforcement letter was identified in the source packet.

LGD-3303 is sold online by research-chemical vendors carrying explicit "for research use only... not for human use" disclaimers, yet the same vendor product pages foreground preclinical rat muscle-sparing and receptor-potency data (e.g., "completely inhibits the loss of muscle weight," nanomolar Ki/EC50 figures) in ways that read as implied bodybuilding or performance benefit. No human efficacy or safety trial, case series, or FDA/DrugBank clinical data for LGD-3303 was located in this session. Muscle-building, bone-density, or other performance/wellness claims circulating in vendor and forum marketing for LGD-3303 are therefore not supported by human evidence and should not be treated as established benefits.
controversies: Vendor pages present rat muscle-sparing data in ways that imply human performance benefit without human evidence.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In a phase IIb, multicentric, randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 149 patients (144 in the full analysis set) with hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers, topical LL-37 (0.5 or 1.6 mg/mL, twice weekly) did not significantly improve complete wound closure versus placebo in the overall population (26.5% and 24.7% vs 25.3%, p>0.05); a post-hoc subgroup analysis in larger ulcers (≥10 cm²) found the 0.5 mg/mL dose significantly improved wound closure (28.1% vs 8.1%, p=0.0458) and healing rate versus placebo. The study drug was reported well tolerated, with six serious adverse events judged possibly (none probably) treatment-related and no deaths.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim reports a negative or conflicting human finding.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: LL-37 is sold online as a research peptide framed around antimicrobial, wound-healing, and 'innate immune response' research applications, but the only substantive human controlled-trial evidence located is a single topical trial in venous leg ulcers whose overall result was negative; no human evidence was identified supporting systemic immune-support, anti-aging, longevity, or general antimicrobial-supplementation uses for which cathelicidin/LL-37 products are informally marketed, and FDA states it lacks sufficient safety information on the compound in humans.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim describes promotional or online certainty beyond the cited evidence.

evidenceGaps: LL-37 is sold by research-chemical/peptide vendors framed around antimicrobial, wound-healing, and 'innate immune response' research applications, but the only substantive human controlled-trial evidence located is a single topical trial in venous leg ulcers whose overall result was negative; no human evidence was identified supporting systemic immune-support, anti-aging, longevity, or general antimicrobial-supplementation uses for which cathelicidin/LL-37 products are informally marketed, and FDA states it lacks sufficient safety information on the compound in humans.
controversies: Post-hoc subgroup benefit in larger ulcers from the 2021 RCT is unconfirmed; gray-market framing treats LL-37 as a general host-defense supplement despite FDA safety caveats.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In a two-year, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial in 1,284 men on ADT for prostate cancer (646 toremifene 80 mg/day, 638 placebo), new vertebral fractures occurred in 2.5% vs 4.9% (relative risk reduction 50%, p = 0.05), and bone mineral density rose at spine, hip and femoral neck (p < 0.0001); venous thromboembolic events were more frequent with toremifene (2.6% vs 1.1%). This supports a bone effect in older ADT-treated men and does not establish efficacy or safety for young men using toremifene for post-cycle recovery.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim reports a negative or conflicting human finding.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Toremifene is promoted on bodybuilding sites as a post-cycle-therapy SERM said to restore natural testosterone, raise free testosterone, prevent gynecomastia and outperform tamoxifen. RxList independently confirms 2026-08-29 that the historical US human Factrel product is discontinued, resolving the narrow question of whether a human gonadorelin product is currently US-marketed (it is not). The claim wording has been updated to state the ovulation-induction indication is Canada-only/historical. claimSpecificEvidence.claim: GSK2881078 is a synthetic, nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) — an indole-carbonitrile small molecule (CAS 1539314-06-1, PubChem CID 86709174) — that acts as an anabolic agent inducing anabolic effects in muscle via the androgen receptor, without approval as a drug product in any jurisdiction.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: High-confidence regulatory, label or agency fact backed by an authoritative source.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In a randomized, placebo-controlled, dose-escalation phase 1 study in healthy older men (1.0-4.0 mg/day) and postmenopausal women (0.35-1.5 mg/day) dosed for 28-56 days, GSK2881078 produced dose-dependent increases in total lean body mass at every dose level versus placebo; women gained roughly 3.39 kg and men roughly 1.76 kg of total lean mass by 8 weeks at studied doses. This is a healthy-volunteer pharmacodynamic finding, not evidence of clinical benefit (e.g., strength, function, or muscle-wasting outcomes) in a patient population.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Human evidence exists but is not settled (was Moderate).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In the same phase 1 study, all GSK2881078-dosed subjects showed reductions in HDL cholesterol (30-45% at the highest doses), and male subjects showed reversible reductions in total testosterone; changes reversed after stopping the drug. No serious adverse events were reported and the compound was described as generally well tolerated in this healthy-volunteer setting, but suppression of HDL cholesterol and androgen axis parameters are class-consistent safety signals for SARMs. An independent clinical-reference source (LiverTox) additionally reports that in this GSK2881078 trial, ALT rose above the upper limit of normal in over 50% of treated subjects (versus 13% of placebo) and above 5x ULN in 3% of treated subjects — a hepatic-transaminase-elevation signal not described in the primary paper's HDL/testosterone results and now added here as a distinct safety-critical signal.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Human evidence exists but is not settled (was Moderate).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: GSK2881078 was studied in a 13-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2a trial (NCT03359473) in 96 dosed COPD patients aged 50-75 with muscle weakness, using sex-specific doses (2 mg/day in men, 1 mg/day in women) alongside a home exercise program, with leg-press strength and DXA lean mass as primary/secondary endpoints. The trial completed in November 2019 with 77 of 96 participants completing and 10 discontinuations attributed to adverse events. The basis for the trial's existence, design and participant disposition in this packet is the trial registration records - the ClinicalTrials.gov entry and the sponsor's own study register, the latter now carrying no usable authority tier - which establish that the trial was conducted and how it was designed, but not what it found; no results from the primary publication have been retrieved and no efficacy outcome is asserted here. The quantitative leg-press and DXA results were not retrieved from a primary publication in this review and are unknown here. A separate, independently accessed companion patient-reported-outcomes study of the same trial (Tabberer et al. 2024) reports that in a qualitative interview subsample (n=32), most participants described improvements in muscle strength and functional limitations and all reported a positive trial experience; this corroborates a general positive direction of participant-perceived effect but does not confirm, quantify, or sex-differentiate the efficacy result, and does not substitute for the primary trial's quantitative endpoints.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim reports a negative or conflicting human finding.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: FDA states that SARMs as a drug class have not been approved by FDA for any use, are illegally marketed (often as dietary supplements, which they are not), and have been linked to life-threatening reactions including liver injury requiring hospitalization and increased risk of heart attack or stroke. This is a class-wide regulatory position; the FDA alert does not name GSK2881078 specifically, and GSK2881078 itself is an investigational compound with no completed marketing application or approved product.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: High-confidence regulatory, label or agency fact backed by an authoritative source.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: GSK2881078 is sold online as a research-use-only compound (not for human consumption), while GSK's own completed trials tested it only under close medical supervision at low, sex-specific microgram/milligram doses for defined short durations (up to 13 weeks) with lab-monitored safety endpoints. No published human evidence supports self-administered, unsupervised, or longer-duration gray-market use for bodybuilding, anti-aging, or general muscle-building purposes, and FDA's SARM-class warnings (heart attack/stroke/liver injury risk) apply to this unsupervised-use pattern.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim describes promotional or online certainty beyond the cited evidence.

evidenceGaps: Primary COPD trial full sex-specific results and some phase-1 PK papers were not fully re-fetched in the source packet; long-term safety is unknown.
No claim-level evidence was sourced this session; only the candidate/evidence-packet identifier-name citation(s) recorded in BIO-LOCAL-007-seed-gap-inventory.md were used to compile this record.
controversies: Online performance marketing may overstate lean-mass findings from short investigational trials.

A secondary source (Wikipedia) states GSK2881078 increased muscle strength in men with COPD but does not confirm an effect in women, while the primary Thorax journal publication reporting full quantitative leg-press/lean-mass results and any sex-differentiated statistical findings could not be accessed in this research pass (PMC/publisher pages returned bot-verification pages). The claim is retained as Limited-tier and review-gated pending direct access to the primary article.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Hexarelin is a synthetic hexapeptide GHRP-class growth hormone secretagogue that stimulates growth hormone release both in vitro and in vivo by acting as a ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHS-R1a) agonist.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Consistent human or authoritative evidence for the stated claim (was Strong).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In a double-blind, placebo-controlled, rising-dose study of 12 healthy adult male volunteers, single intravenous boluses of hexarelin (0.5, 1, and 2 micrograms/kg) produced dose-dependent increases in plasma growth hormone, peaking at about 30 minutes; mean peak GH concentrations were 3.9 (placebo), 26.9, 52.3, and 55.0 ng/mL at increasing doses, with response near-maximal by the 2 microgram/kg dose. This is an acute GH-release pharmacodynamic finding in healthy men, not evidence of any downstream clinical benefit.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Human evidence exists but is not settled (was Moderate).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In a rat model of myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury (left coronary artery ligation), subcutaneous hexarelin (100 mcg/kg/day for 7 days) improved cardiac systolic function, reduced malondialdehyde production, and increased surviving cardiomyocytes versus control, an effect blocked by a GHSR antagonist and attributed to interleukin-1 pathway modulation. This is preclinical rodent data and does not establish a cardioprotective effect in humans.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim reports a negative or conflicting human finding.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Hexarelin has no FDA-approved drug product and, unlike some other GH secretagogue peptides (e.g. ipamorelin, GHRP-6), does not currently appear on FDA's published Category 2 list of bulk drug substances that may present significant safety risks for compounding; its regulatory status for 503A/503B compounding has not been affirmatively confirmed and should be re-checked against the live FDA list at review time.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Human evidence exists but is not settled (was Moderate).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: The WADA 2026 Prohibited List names examorelin (hexarelin) under S2.2.4 Growth hormone releasing factors, among the GH-releasing peptides, so it is prohibited in sport at all times.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: High-confidence regulatory, label or agency fact backed by an authoritative source.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Hexarelin (CAS 140703-51-1) is catalogued in PubChem under the synonym Examorelin (CID 6918297) with molecular formula C47H58N12O6.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Consistent human or authoritative evidence for the stated claim (was Strong).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Hexarelin is promoted online with a broad list of purported human benefits -- faster recovery and hypertrophy, increased lipolysis, joint/tendon healing, improved sleep, cardioprotection, and bone/skin effects from 'multi-cycle use' -- none of which are supported by controlled human trial evidence located in this review; the only controlled human data available addresses acute growth-hormone pharmacodynamics, and the cardioprotection claim specifically originates from a rat ischemia/reperfusion study, not human outcomes data.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim describes promotional or online certainty beyond the cited evidence.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In a dose-response study of intravenous hexarelin (0-1.0 micrograms/kg) in healthy adult men (Massoud et al. 1996, J Clin Endocrinol Metab), hexarelin produced dose-dependent increases in prolactin (up to 180% above baseline, ED50 0.39 micrograms/kg) and a step increase in cortisol of approximately 40% at doses of 0.5 micrograms/kg and above, in addition to growth hormone release. In a separate 16-week chronic twice-daily subcutaneous dosing study (Rahim et al. 1999, Clinical Endocrinology), the cortisol response to hexarelin decreased over the treatment course and prolactin levels remained stable, with the authors concluding that clinically significant over-stimulation of the pituitary-adrenal axis and prolactin secretion did not occur at the doses used. Taken together, hexarelin has demonstrated measurable acute effects on cortisol and prolactin beyond the GH axis, though the only located chronic-dosing study did not find clinically significant HPA-axis over-stimulation at the studied dose.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim reports a negative or conflicting human finding.

evidenceGaps: Human evidence is largely limited to acute IV pharmacodynamic studies; chronic subcutaneous self-use safety/efficacy is not established.

Vendor marketing content presents hexarelin's CD36-mediated cardioprotection as an established effect ('cardioprotective effects in ischemia-reperfusion and heart failure studies'), while the only located supporting study is a rat ischemia/reperfusion model; no human cardioprotection trial was found in this pass.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In a 2-year, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial in 65 healthy adults aged 60-81, oral MK-677 25 mg/day significantly increased fat-free mass relative to placebo at 1 year (change +1.1 kg vs -0.5 kg, P<0.001) and increased body cell mass, but produced no significant change in abdominal visceral fat or total fat mass, and the increase in fat-free mass did not translate into improved strength or physical function.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: No ibutamoren product is FDA-approved for any indication, and vendor/clinic marketing commonly claims broad benefits - enhanced muscle protein synthesis, improved deep/REM sleep, faster recovery from workouts and surgery, youthful skin and hair, slower biological aging, fat loss, joint health, and elevated mood via serotonin/dopamine - that are not supported by the identified controlled human evidence, which comes from a single trial in older adults showing increased fat-free mass but no functional/strength benefit, adverse metabolic signals (higher fasting glucose, lower insulin sensitivity), and a separate FDA-flagged cardiac safety signal from an unrelated trial population.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Kisspeptin-10 is the minimal bioactive C-terminal decapeptide fragment of the KISS1 gene product (kisspeptin/metastin) and acts as an agonist at the KISS1R (GPR54) receptor, the key upstream activator of hypothalamic GnRH neurons in the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Consistent human or authoritative evidence for the stated claim (was Strong).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In its Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee briefing document, FDA concluded the evaluation criteria weigh against placing kisspeptin-10 on the 503A Bulks List, citing poor physicochemical characterization (impurity data not publicly available or provided in the certificate of analysis), potential immunogenicity risk from parenteral administration of a 10-amino-acid peptide (amplified by possible aggregation and peptide-related impurities), and insufficient evidence of effectiveness for treating hypogonadism in men via IM or SC administration.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: High-confidence regulatory, label or agency fact backed by an authoritative source.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In a controlled human pharmacodynamic study in healthy men, intravenous kisspeptin-10 produced a rapid, dose-dependent rise in serum LH after bolus dosing (maximal effect at 1 microg/kg), and continuous low-dose infusion (1.5 microg/kg/h) increased LH pulse frequency and raised testosterone from 16.6 +/- 2.4 to 24.0 +/- 2.5 nmol/L; the authors describe this as evidence for its potential as a stimulator of endogenous reproductive hormone secretion, not as a demonstrated treatment for any diagnosed condition.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Preliminary human evidence with documented limits (was Limited).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: No FDA-approved kisspeptin-10 product exists, and FDA's own compounding evaluation found insufficient evidence that kisspeptin-10 is effective for treating hypogonadism in men; the acute LH/testosterone-stimulating pharmacodynamic effects shown in short research-clinic infusion studies have not been shown to translate into a validated clinical treatment for hypogonadism, infertility, or libido disorders, and no chronic self-administration safety or efficacy data in gray-market users exist.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim describes promotional or online certainty beyond the cited evidence.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Kisspeptin-10 is promoted online for fertility, weight loss, mood, anxiety and cognition, far beyond the small acute human LH-stimulation studies; FDA's compounding review found insufficient evidence of effectiveness for hypogonadism in men. Anecdotal reports are not treated as evidence.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Support is user, community or case reports, not generalizable evidence.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: Kisspeptin-10 (human) is registered in PubChem as CID 25240297 with molecular formula C63H83N17O14, corresponding to the C-terminal 10-amino-acid fragment of the KISS1 gene product (metastin/kisspeptin), CAS number 374675-21-5.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Consistent human or authoritative evidence for the stated claim (was Strong).

evidenceGaps: Human data are largely short pharmacodynamic infusion studies; chronic disease-endpoint evidence and gray-market self-use safety are lacking.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In vitro, nanomolar concentrations of KPV inhibit NF-kappaB and MAP kinase inflammatory signaling and reduce pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion in human intestinal epithelial cell lines and T cells, and KPV is taken up into cells via the peptide transporter PepT1.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Human evidence exists but is not settled (was Moderate).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: In the Dalmasso et al. 2008 (Gastroenterology) study, C57BL/6 mouse models of DSS- and TNBS-induced colitis showed that oral administration of KPV in drinking water reduced colitis incidence and inflammatory markers (including myeloperoxidase activity and pro-inflammatory cytokine expression); a second, independent 2008 study (Dalmasso et al., Inflammatory Bowel Diseases, PMID 18092346) corroborates similar anti-inflammatory effects of KPV in DSS-colitis and CD45RB-transfer-colitis mouse models, including significantly reduced myeloperoxidase activity and improved recovery. This is animal-model evidence only, not evidence of efficacy in humans.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Preliminary human evidence with documented limits (was Limited).

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: FDA lists KPV in the 'bulk drug substances nominated but withdrawn' table for 503A compounding evaluation, stating it has not identified any human exposure data for KPV administered via any route and lacks information on whether KPV would cause harm if administered to humans.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: High-confidence regulatory, label or agency fact backed by an authoritative source.

claimSpecificEvidence.claim: No completed human clinical trials of KPV have been identified; published efficacy and mechanism evidence for KPV's anti-inflammatory effects is limited to animal (mouse) colitis and dermatitis models and in vitro human cell-line experiments, leaving human efficacy and safety for gut-health, skin, and general anti-inflammatory uses unestablished despite active consumer marketing of KPV for those uses.
claimSpecificEvidence.gradeRationale: Claim describes promotional or online certainty beyond the cited evidence.

evidenceGaps: No completed human clinical trial evidence for KPV efficacy or safety was located.

controversies: PCAC committee vote dynamics versus FDA staff recommendation create unresolved regulatory trajectory questions while consumer marketing continues.

FDA staff's PCAC briefing document (fda.gov/media/193346/download) recommended against adding KPV to the 503A Bulks List, but the July 23-24, 2026 PCAC committee voted 8 Yes / 6 No / 1 Abstain to recommend inclusion despite that staff recommendation and despite documented absence of human safety data; this advisory tension is material to the compound's regulatory trajectory and is not resolved by the current (unchanged) live FDA withdrawn-nomination page.
